source_text: Δοκεῖ μοι οὖν μετρίως κατεσκευάσθαι οὐ μόνον ὅτι γεννηθήσεται ἐκ παρθένου ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν ἀλλ᾿ ὅτι καὶ προφῆται ἦσαν ἐν Ἰουδαίοις, προλέγοντες οὐ μόνον τὰ καθολικὰ περὶ μελλόντων, ὡς τὰ περὶ Χριστοῦ καὶ τὰ περὶ βασιλειῶν κοσμικῶν καὶ περὶ τῶν συμβησομένων τῷ Ἰσραὴλ καὶ περὶ τῶν πιστευόντων τῷ σωτῆρι ἐθνῶν καὶ πολλῶν ἄλλων τῶν περὶ αὐτοῦ λεχθέντων, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ καθ᾿ ἕνα, ὡς περὶ τῶν ὄνων Κὶς ἀπολομένων, πῶς εὑρεθήσονται, καὶ περὶ τῆς νόσου, ἧς ἐνόσησεν ὁ τοῦ βασιλέως Ἰσραὴλ υἱὸς, ἢ εἴ τι ἄλλο ἀναγέγραπται τοιοῦτον. ἔτι δὲ πρὸς Ἕλληνας λεκτέον, ἀπειθοῦντας τῇ ἐκ παρθένου γενέσει τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, ὅτι ὁ δημιουργὸς ἐν τῇ τῶν ποικίλων ζῴων γενέσει ἔδειξεν ὅτι ἦν αὐτῷ βουληθέντι δυνατὸν ποιῆσαι ὅπερ ἐφ᾿ ἑνὸς ζῴου καὶ ἐπ᾿ ἄλλων καὶ ἐπ᾿ αὐτῶν τῶν ἀνθρώπων. εὑρίσκεται δέ τινα τῶν ζῴων θήλεα, μὴ ἔχοντα ἄῤῥενος κοινωνίαν. ὡς οἱ περὶ ζῴων ἀναγράψαντες λέγουσι περὶ γυπῶν· καὶ τοῦτο τὸ ζῷον χωρὶς μίξεως σῴζει τὴν διαδοχὴν τῶν γενῶν. τί οὖν παράδοξον, εἰ βουληθεὶς ὁ θεὸς θεῖόν τινα διδάσκαλον πέμψαι τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων πεποίηκεν ἀντὶ σπερματικοῦ λόγου, τοῦ· ἐκ μίξεως τῶν ἀῤῥένων ταῖς γυναιξὶ, [ποιῆσαι] ἄλλῳ τρόπῳ γενέσθαι τὸν λόγον τοῦ τεχθησομένου: καὶ κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς δὲ τοὺς Ἕλληνας οὐ πάντες ἄνθρωποι ἐξ ἀνδρὸς καὶ γυναικὸς ἐγένοντο. εἰ γὰρ γενητός ἐστιν ὁ κόσμος, ὡς καὶ πολλοῖς Ἑλλήνων ἤρεσεν, ἀνάγκη τοὺς πρώτους μὴ ἐκ συνουσίας γεγονέναι ἀλλ᾿ ἀπὸ γῆς, σπερματικῶν λόγων συστάντων ἐν τῇ γῇ· ὅπερ οἶμαι παραδοξότερον εἶναι τοῦ ἐξ ἡμίσους ὁμοίως τοῖς λοιποῖς ἀνθρώποις γενέσθαι τὸν Ἰησοῦν. οὐδὲν δ᾿ ἄτοπον πρὸς Ἕλληνας καὶ Ἑλληνικαῖς ἱστορίαις χρήσασθαι, ἵνα μὴ δοκῶμεν μόνοι τῇ παραδόξῳ ἱστορίᾳ ταύτῃ κεχρῆσθαι. Ἔδοξε γάρ τισιν οὐ περὶ ἀρχαίων τινῶν ἱστοριῶν καὶ ἡρωϊκῶν ἀλλὰ καὶ περί τινων χθὲς καὶ πρώην γενομένων ἀναγράψαι ὡς δυνατὸν ὅτι καὶ Πλάτων ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀμφικτιόνης γέγονε, κωλυθέντος τοῦ Ἀρίστωνος αὐτῇ συνελθεῖν, ἕως ἀποκυήσει τὸν ἐξ Ἀπόλλωνος σπαρέντα. ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν ἀληθῶς μῦθοι, κινήσαντες εἰς τὸ ἀναπλάσαι τοιοῦτό τι περὶ ἀνδρὸς, ὃν ἐνόμιζον μείζονα τῶν πολλῶν ἔχοντα σοφίαν καὶ δύναμιν καὶ ἀπὸ κρειττόνων καὶ θειοτέρων σπερμάτων τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς συστάσεως τοῦ σώματος εἰληφέναι, ὡς τοῦθ᾿ ἁρμόζον τοῖς μείζοσιν ἢ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον, ἐπεὶ δὲ τὸν Ἰουδαῖον ὁ Κέλσος εἰσήγαγε διαλεγόμενον τῷ Ἰησοῦ καὶ διασύροντα τὴν, ὡς οἴεται, προσποίησιν τῆς ἐκ παρθένου γενέσεως αὐτοῦ, φέροντα τοὺς Ἑλληνικοὺς μύθους περὶ Δανάης καὶ Μελανίππης καὶ Αὔγης καὶ Ἀντιόπης, λεκτέον ὅτι ταῦτα βωμολόχῳ ἔπρεπε τὰ ῥήματα καὶ οὐ σπουδάζοντι ἐν τῇ ἀπαγγελίᾳ.
pass_a_gloss: It seems to me that it has been moderately demonstrated not only that our Savior will be born from a virgin, but also that there were prophets among the Jews, foretelling not only the general things about the future, such as those about Christ and those about worldly kingdoms and those about the things that will happen to Israel and those about the nations that will believe in the Savior and many other things that were said about him, but also the specific things, such as those about the donkeys of Kish that were lost, how they will be found, and about the illness that the son of King Israel had, or if anything else of this kind has been written. And yet, it must be spoken to the Greeks, who disbelieve the birth of Jesus from a virgin, that the Creator showed in the generation of various animals that it was possible for Him to do what He willed for one animal and for others and for humans themselves. For some of the animals, females are found that do not have male companionship. As those who have written about animals say about vultures, this animal preserves the succession of its kind without mixing. What is paradoxical, then, if God, willing to send some divine teacher to the human race, has made the word of the one to be born to come about in a different way instead of the seminal word, which is from the mixing of males with females? And according to the Greeks themselves, not all humans were born from a man and a woman. For if the world is generated, as many Greeks have thought, it is necessary that the first humans were not from cohabitation but from the earth, with seminal words constituting them in the earth, which I think is more paradoxical than for Jesus to be born from a virgin in a similar way to other humans. There is nothing inappropriate in using Greek histories to address the Greeks, so that we may not seem to be the only ones using this paradoxical history. For some have thought it right not only to write about ancient histories and heroic deeds but also about some things that happened yesterday and the day before, such as that Plato was born from Amphiction, when Ariston was prevented from having intercourse with her, until she gave birth to the one sown by Apollo. But these things are truly myths, moving them to fabricate something similar about a man whom they thought had greater wisdom and power and had taken the beginning of his bodily constitution from better and more divine seeds, as if this were fitting for those who are greater than human. And since the Jew introduced by Celsus, conversing with Jesus and disparaging, as he thinks, the addition of his birth from a virgin, brings up the Greek myths about Danae and Melanippe and Auge and Antiope, it must be said that these words are suitable for a buffoon and not for one who is serious in his proclamation.
pass_b_english: It seems to me that the case has been reasonably established: not only will our Savior be born of a virgin, but there were also prophets among the Jews who foretold far more than just the broad outlines of the future. They spoke of Christ, of worldly kingdoms, of what would befall Israel, of the nations that would believe in the Savior, and of many other matters concerning him. Beyond these general predictions, they also foretold specific details—how Kish’s lost donkeys would be found, the illness that struck the son of Israel’s king, and anything else of that sort that stands recorded.

We must also address the Greeks, who refuse to believe in Jesus’ virgin birth. The Creator demonstrated in the generation of various animals that He could accomplish whatever He willed—not only for a single species, but for others and for human beings themselves. Certain female animals, as naturalists report, reproduce without any male partner; vultures, for instance, preserve their kind without mating. So what is so paradoxical if God, intending to send a divine teacher to humanity, caused the Logos of the one to be born to come into being by a different means instead of the seminal word that comes from the union of male and female?

Even according to the Greeks’ own accounts, not all humans originated from a man and a woman. If the world was generated, as many Greeks held, then the first human beings could not have come from sexual union; they had to arise from the earth, constituted by seminal logoi implanted in it. That strikes me as far more paradoxical than Jesus being born of a virgin in a manner essentially like that of other humans.

There is nothing out of place in appealing to Greek histories when speaking to Greeks, so that we do not appear to be the only ones relying on a paradoxical story. Some writers thought it worth recording not only ancient and heroic tales but also events of the very recent past—for example, that Plato was born of Amphictione after Ariston was prevented from lying with her until she gave birth to the child sown by Apollo. But these are plainly myths, invented to glorify a man they believed surpassed others in wisdom and power, crediting his bodily origin to superior, more divine seed—as if such a pedigree befitted those greater than ordinary mortals.

Now Celsus introduces a Jew who confronts Jesus and mocks, as he supposes, the claim of his virgin birth by dragging in the Greek myths about Danaë, Melanippe, Auge, and Antiope. The response must be that such talk suits a buffoon, not someone who is serious in his proclamation.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that maintains the theological and historical distinctions (e.g., 'seminal logoi' vs 'seminal word', 'buffoon' vs 'bwo-lochos'). All specific details regarding the donkeys of Kish, the illness of the king's son, and the Greek myths (Danae, Melanippe, Auge, Antiope) are correctly preserved.
